Messages.Author: Loughman
Messages.Body:
I guess I've led a sheltered existence. I had never seen so many
Parity Shifts in one place as I did at the NAC this last weekend,
especially on Day Two. The removal of PTO from play has opened up a
significantly wider variety of vamps and decks for tournament play.
After seeing the profound effect Parity Shift had on several tables,
and the extensive counter-measures other decks had to contain to deal
with the possibility of being Shifted, I find myself wondering if it
is a good card to keep in the game. Few cards have such a significant
swing in pool and decks designed to employ several of them have no
problem spending enough pool (and gaining permanent resources) to
shift again in a very short time.

Has any one else noticed this too? I'm not one for banning cards for a
frivolous reason (and I was running 3 Shifts in my deck sunday) but
maybe this one has outlived it's usefulness.

say, a Revolutionary Council).

which is huge.

Now, what can be done to counter this ?

- give the Sabbatics a vote that, without being a copycat, will also give
them some harming + pooling options

- create a counter card for Parity Shift, as Villein is to Minion Tap (would
be an elegant solution which, if well balanced, wouldn't wallpaperize the
card)

- make it "once par game per methuselah" looks like a satisfying solution

The last 2 solutions would allow for the creation of new, good cards, less
powerful than PS is right now yet useful.

The idea of a vote (or vote modifiers �-la-Voter Cap) allowing non-bouncers
to survive big bleeders and still harm their prey is good. Now, it has to
stay balanced, and the restriction to Cammie titles only hurts the
opposition. Hence the necessity to find a balance, either by tuning PS down
or tuning the Sabbat voters up.

Messages.Author: frubeng
Messages.Body:
Banning a powerful card because it is being used is ridiculous. In
that case, we should have banned Blood doll as it was the most
powerful master card (still is i think, although reduced in power/use
by vessel). I also think Banishment is stronger than parity shift.

Parity shift has many requirements:
1. Prince/justicar: From a deckbuilding standpoint, it is much harder
to establish votelock with purely those titles than it would be with
cardinals, Inner circles or cards such as Legacy of Pander/foundation
exhibit etc.
This goes with the comparison of Political stranglehold/reigns/ancient
which can be called by the 1-cap vampire supporting the fatties.
2. You have to be at lower pool than the target, this means
essentially that it is not an ousting mechanism. This also mean it is
generally very hard or inconvenient to call more than one per turn.
Further, to use parity efficiently, you must be low pool and thus
playing dangerously.
3. You cannot target yourself or give pool back to the one who was
targeted, making it less flexible.

Decks centered around parity shift are not overpowered, and banning it/
making it OPG would destroy them, reducing the variety of the game.
Any vote deck using princes would become suboptimal.

I really don't like bans or impactful erratas. I beleive if there was
really an issue, the way Orpheus is proposing sounds much more
interesting (to create other cards to compete); but i really don't
think there is an issue.

From a new player's perspective Parity Shift is both a very strong
card and hard to get a hold of. If the card is not banned or changed

vote cards as an effective swing of 10 pool is huge. And again if it
is restricted to one per game per Methuselah then needless to say
Prince decks may likely be less interesting for people to focus on for
vote. Should that serve as an indicator for how powerful the card
really is? If it were so easy to deal with and provide a good
replacement, solution, etc. then it would have already been done. That
being said I would be surprised if something didn't change January
1st, 2010 as this is the only card I ever hear bout being so powerful.

Messages.Author: Dai
Messages.Body:
The problem seems to be that, since Parity Shift has been out of
ciculation since CE, while some of the later players are obviously
aware of the card, it's not something that they prepare for in their
normal casual/ semi-casual metagame. There hasn't been a hard focus on
the Camarilla for several years either, between CE and KoT. In that
time, without Parity Shift and without the Cam vampires available
(well, I haven't played for a while to know if BSC made an impact),
players wouldn't sit at tables with 3-4 Cam princes decks and wouldn't
need to really prepare for it to enjoy their games.

This is a card that has been a part of the game since the very
beginning. It's a little surprising that people still see it as a
problem that needs a fix. If it truly needed to be fixed, wouldn't it
have been fixed already at some point in the past 12+ years?

Practically every decktype has some available answer to Parity Shift,
be it intercept, action cancel, vote cancel, votes, rush, etc... You
can also play around Parity Shift, if you are the prey, by trying to
keep under your predator.

It's an action that the prince/ justicar must take himself, opening
himself to intercept and combat, possibly being burned. The player
must make a significant pool investment to get things running and is
in trouble if unpleasantry befalls that investment. A 7-10 pool
investment that needs some stealth and some way of surviving a fight.

Parity Shift vs. the weenies is a significant balance issue that needs
to be addressed by those who see the card as a problem. The
exclusivity of Parity Shift to Camarilla is not a concerning issue.

A 1 cap can call a KRC for 4 pool damage. Parity Shift needs a likely
7+ cap prince/ justicar to do 5 pool damage, but is also contingent on
so many other factors and perhaps can't target the players you want to
target, and you will seldom be able to call so many on the same
target. If a 1 cap is removed, any other vampire can call that KRC. If
your prince is removed or loses his title, your vote, your stealth,
your vote push and your vote cap all sit in your hand.

Cheers,

Dai

The issue of why a card is or isn't reprinted kind of boils down to
reading the minds of people at White Wolf who make these decisions.
I've noticed they seldom ever talk about what leads them to ever make
any individual reprint-or-not-reprint decision so we have to speculate
about them.

I think some of it boils down to that they don't really want to
reprint every card because it undercuts the collectibility of older
sets (and hence a current set's collectibility - since it will
someday become an "older set") and because the more work you spend
reprinting older cards, the less time you have to spend on newer
cards - which are what sell the most. So if they don't want to
reprint all cards, some of them have to not be reprinted. Which
ones are those?

You'd think they'd reprint all the real important cards but they
don't always seem to. Again, this may be to avoid undercutting the
collectibility of older sets. If you're guranteed that every card
of importance will always be reprinted, you don't need to work that
hard to get an older copy. You can just kick back and wait until
they reprint it. But if you're not really sure, then maybe you'd
better work on getting a copy now before the existing supply gets
even older and harder to find. Or maybe they will reprint it -
but not anytime soon, in which case making the choice to wait will
cause you to have to do without for an unknown period of time. All
of these factors will cause players to value older sets more than
if White Wolf reprints every significant card on a timely basis.

Another reason could be simply that it's very hard to make these
decisions without leaving out an important candidate for repriting
from time to time. Are they really so organized about their
reprint decisions that they're aware when a card like Parity Shift
is passing through the net? Quite possibly not.

Or maybe they're in process of evaluting the card. It's not much
of a stretch to think Parity Shift is on the "watch list" of cards
to consider banning or altering. If so, they may be reluctant to
reprint it just before it's a about to be changed or banned.

Or maybe the problem is the artwork. Although not being able to
use the existing artwork ultimately doesn't prevent them from
reprinting a card, getting new artwork that's appropriate to the
card may be a P-I-T-A and tend to cause them to hold back on
reprinting it in any particular set.

Other problems are also possible. One would have expected Parity
Shift to get reprinted in Keepers of Tradition and maybe it had
been slated to be reprinted in that set - then got scrubbed at the
last minute due to any number of technical problems.

The bottom line is, there's all sorts of possible reasons. We
may never know which ones apply unless Parity Shift is banned in
December for next year or reprinted in Heirs to the Blood. And
even then, I doubt we'll know that much more. *shrug*

> To errata the card would nearly take
> the card out of the game (or maybe 1 per game isn't a bad idea).

That depends on the errata. I always hate it when they reprint a
card like Tomb of Ramses III to go from overpowered to pretty much
total dreck. On the other hand, I'm not that keen when they
errata a card in a way that really doesn't mean very much - like
the blood cost to untap in Second Tradition. That just means the
older copies of Second Tradition don't have the right card text but,
at the same time, the errata didn't accomplish much of anything.
The best errata I've ever seen (apart from WwEF) is Mind Rape.
They took a truly overpowered card and turned it into something
that's still quite interesting and useful but much more reasonable.

Fred
